name: Exoplanet Atmosphere Spectroscopy
use: Reading the chemistry of planets around other stars
what: Working out which gases surround a planet orbiting another star from the starlight that passes through its atmosphere. JWST has detected carbon dioxide, water vapour and other molecules on exoplanets this way.
how: As the planet crosses its star, a thin ring of starlight filters through the atmosphere; each molecule absorbs specific infrared wavelengths, leaving a fingerprint in the spectrum.

name: Europa Clipper
use: Assessing whether an ocean moon could support life
what: NASA spacecraft launched in October 2024 to study Jupiter's moon Europa, which hides a salt-water ocean beneath its ice. It arrives in 2030 and will judge whether that ocean could be habitable.
how: Dozens of close flybys with ice-penetrating radar, a mass spectrometer, a dust analyser and cameras map the ice shell and sample material thrown up near the surface.

name: Habitable Worlds Observatory
use: Directly imaging Earth-like planets and searching them for life
what: NASA's planned flagship telescope for photographing Earth-sized planets around Sun-like stars and searching their light for signs of life. It is in early design, targeted for the 2040s.
how: A large, ultra-stable space telescope with a coronagraph that suppresses the star's glare by around ten billion times, so the faint planet beside it can be seen and its spectrum taken.

name: Agnostic Life Detection
use: Recognising life that does not use DNA or proteins
what: Ways to recognise life without assuming it works like Earth life — for example by measuring how molecularly complex a sample is, on the proposal that complex molecules in abundance are very hard to make without biology.
how: Mass spectrometry scores molecular complexity (assembly theory proposes a threshold for this, and it is still debated); other approaches look for chemical disequilibrium or a strong left/right-handedness bias in molecules.

name: Extremophile Research
use: Mapping where life could survive on other worlds
what: Studying organisms that thrive in boiling vents, acid, ice, high radiation and deep rock. They set the known limits of life and so define which places on Mars, Europa or Enceladus are worth searching.
how: Sampling from Earth analogue sites — hydrothermal vents, Antarctic lakes, deep mines — followed by lab culturing and genome sequencing to find how each organism survives.

name: Technosignature Search (SETI)
use: Looking for evidence of technology beyond Earth
what: Searching for signs of technology elsewhere — radio beacons, laser pulses or industrial pollution — rather than biology. Breakthrough Listen is the largest such survey to date and has found no confirmed signal.
how: Radio telescopes scan millions of frequency channels for very narrow-band signals that natural sources do not produce; software filters out interference from Earth's own transmitters.

name: Habitable-Zone Planet Census
what: A curated catalogue of confirmed planets inside the conservative and optimistic liquid-water zones, used to prioritise follow-up spectroscopy and to estimate the frequency of temperate terrestrial worlds.
how: Radial-velocity and transit detections are combined with stellar luminosity models to compute incident flux, and planets are filtered by radius and equilibrium temperature.

name: PLATO Exoplanet Survey
what: A multi-camera space photometer designed to detect and characterise planets around bright, nearby stars, with particular sensitivity to Earth-size worlds in the habitable zone. Its seismology channel simultaneously ages the host stars.
how: An array of off-axis refracting telescopes images the same field, combining photometric precision with a very wide dynamic range for bright hosts.

name: ARIEL Atmospheric Survey
what: A dedicated survey observatory that will build a statistically meaningful sample of exoplanet spectra rather than studying single objects, enabling population-level conclusions about atmospheric diversity.
how: A passively cooled telescope feeding a spectrometer covers the near- and mid-infrared, using the host star as a calibration reference during every observation.

name: Microlensing Planet Survey
what: A wide-field infrared survey that uses gravitational microlensing to find planets at separations and masses that transit and radial-velocity methods cannot reach, including free-floating worlds.
how: A planet orbiting the lens star perturbs the magnification light curve; high-cadence infrared photometry from space resolves the perturbation against the Galactic bulge background.

name: Coronagraphic Direct Imaging
what: Ground-based extreme adaptive optics now images young, self-luminous giant planets and accretion disks around nearby stars, and measures their spectra and astrometry.
how: Thousands of actuators correct atmospheric turbulence in real time, then a coronagraph and post-processing algorithms subtract the residual stellar halo.

name: Extremely Large Telescope Imaging
what: A thirty-nine metre class segmented telescope that will deliver an order-of-magnitude gain in contrast and collecting area for direct characterisation of exoplanets and protoplanetary disks.
how: A segmented primary with integrated adaptive optics feeds high-resolution spectrographs, enabling spectral deconvolution of planet light from residual starlight.

name: Exoplanet Radio Emission Search
what: Low-frequency arrays attempt to detect coherent radio emission from star-planet interactions, which would directly measure an exoplanet magnetic field, a key shield for habitability.
how: Auroral cyclotron maser emission is predicted below a few hundred megahertz; long integrations and beamforming isolate the star system from confusion limits.

name: Radial-Velocity Precision Spectroscopy
what: Ultra-stable spectrographs on large telescopes now measure stellar reflex velocities at the metre-per-second level, supplying the masses that transit surveys cannot determine alone.
how: Light is dispersed across thousands of lines in a simultaneous reference channel; laser frequency combs or thorium-argon calibration track instrumental drift to centimetres per second.

name: Astrometric Planet Census
what: A whole-sky astrometric mission delivered precision parallaxes, proper motions and the first astrometric exoplanet detections, anchoring the mass-luminosity scale used by every other detection method.
how: Two telescopes scan the sky on a continuously changing angle, and global iterative solutions fit positions, parallaxes and orbital wobble simultaneously.

name: Exomoon Detection
what: Transit timing and duration variations are now used to test for moons and trojan companions around transiting planets, a discipline that would expand the habitable real estate of known systems.
how: A moon induces small periodic offsets in transit centre time and duration; long-baseline photometry plus transit-shape modelling recovers the perturbation against stellar noise.

name: Atmospheric Retrieval Pipelines
what: Bayesian and neural retrieval codes invert spectra into temperature profiles, molecular abundances, cloud decks and limb darkening, including rigorous false-positive accounting.
how: Radiative transfer forward models are sampled with nested sampling or simulation-based inference to produce posterior distributions over atmospheric parameters.

name: Venus Cloud Chemistry
what: Detections and non-detections of phosphine and sulphur species in the Venusian cloud deck have driven a rigorous re-examination of whether the middle cloud layer could host microbial life.
how: Ground-based and orbital spectroscopy of Venusian atmospheric windows is combined with photochemical models that test whether observed abundances require an unknown source.

name: Mars Methane Monitoring
what: Two independent spacecraft measure methane and its isotopic ratios at Mars, constraining whether episodic releases are geological, biological or instrumental artefacts.
how: Laser heterodyne and infrared solar occultation spectrometry resolve methane, ethane and carbon isotopes at parts-per-trillion levels from orbit and from the surface.

name: JUICE Icy Moon Tour
what: A European spacecraft in cruise phase will enter orbit around Ganymede after flybys of Callisto and Europa, carrying the most complete remote-sensing payload yet sent to the Jovian system.
how: Ice-penetrating radar, laser altimetry, magnetometry and submillimetre spectrometry are combined to infer ocean depth and detect internal liquid layers.

name: Dragonfly Titan Rotorcraft
what: A nuclear-powered rotorcraft will hop between sites on Titan, sampling prebiotic surface chemistry across hundreds of kilometres rather than at a single landing point.
how: Eight rotors allow multi-kilometre flights in the dense low-gravity atmosphere; a mass spectrometer and chemical analyser characterise organics at each landing site.

name: ExoMars Rosalind Franklin Rover
what: A rover with a two-metre drill will sample Martian subsurface material shielded from radiation and oxidants, the most favourable environment for preserved organic molecules.
how: A rotary-percussive drill extracts cores from beneath the oxidised layer; a mass spectrometer and Raman instrument then analyse them inside a sealed laboratory.

name: Venus Life Finder
what: A series of small, low-cost probes designed to descend through the Venusian cloud deck and measure organic chemistry and droplet composition directly, rather than spectroscopically.
how: A compact entry vehicle carries a fluorescence-based organic detector and a cloud-particle analyser, using a small dedicated launch vehicle to keep mission cost low.

name: Uranus Orbiter and Probe
what: The highest-priority planetary flagship concept will place an orbiter and an atmospheric entry probe at Uranus, sampling primordial composition preserved since solar system formation.
how: The orbiter carries magnetometry, a Narrow-angle imager and mass spectrometry; the probe descends under a parachute transmitting composition data before the pressure and heat kill it.

name: Enceladus Orbilander
what: A proposed mission that would both orbit and land at Enceladus, collecting fresh plume material ejected from its subsurface ocean and analysing it for biosignature patterns.
how: Plume flyby sampling at kilometres per second is followed by a landing phase that collects fall-out material and runs life-detection instruments directly on ocean-derived ice.

name: Cryobot Subsurface Ocean Access
what: Thermal and hybrid melting probes are being developed to descend through kilometres of ice shell and reach liquid water directly, the only way to verify ocean habitability in situ.
how: A nuclear or radioisotope heat source melts a descending borehole, with a tether carrying power and data; hybrid designs add a mechanical cutting head for debris layers.

name: Ice-Penetrating Radar Sounding
what: Low-frequency radar sounders on planetary spacecraft map internal ice layering, basal topography and the presence of liquid water beneath ice shells and polar caps.
how: Radar waves penetrate ice with low loss and reflect from dielectric contrasts at the ice-water or ice-rock interface, with coherent processing resolving depth.

name: Biosignature False-Positive Framework
what: A structured standard for deciding which atmospheric detections can reasonably be called biosignatures, requiring abiotic explanations to be explicitly quantified before any claim is made.
how: A catalogue of known abiotic production pathways and photochemical models is applied to each candidate spectrum, and the surviving explanatory gap is reported rather than the raw detection.

name: Space-Radiation Extremophile Survivability
what: Long-duration exposure platforms outside spacecraft test whether spores, lichens and biofilms survive vacuum, ultraviolet and cosmic radiation, directly bounding panspermia and forward-contamination risk.
how: Samples are mounted on external facility trays with dosimetry and are returned for viability assays; organic degradation is tracked spectroscopically in parallel.

name: Hydrothermal Vent Origin-of-Life Chemistry
what: Laboratory reactors reproducing alkaline hydrothermal vent conditions generate organic molecules and proton gradients without enzymes, the leading candidate for the energy source of the first metabolism.
how: Microfluidic and high-pressure reactors precipitate iron-sulphide membranes across a pH gradient and drive carbon fixation and phosphorylation chemistry.

name: Interstellar Probe Mission
what: An interstellar probe is a fast, lightweight spacecraft aimed past the heliosphere to sample the local interstellar medium directly, rather than inferring it from remote sensing. It is the first mission class designed to leave the Sun's influence while still returning data.
how: The architecture combines a radioisotope power source, a high-gain antenna for communication across hundreds of astronomical units, and a trajectory that uses a Jupiter gravity assist or a solar Oberth manoeuvre. Transit to the heliopause takes decades, so instrument autonomy and power longevity dominate the design.
companies: Johns Hopkins University Applied Physics Laboratory

name: Solar Gravitational Lens Telescope
what: A spacecraft parked in the solar gravitational focal region uses the Sun itself as an optical lens with an effective aperture of roughly a million kilometres. That gain is enough in principle to resolve surface features on an exoplanet tens of light years away.
how: Light from a distant system is bent by solar gravity and converges along a focal line extending outward from about 550 astronomical units, where a modest telescope collects it. The image arrives as an Einstein ring that must be computationally inverted, and the spacecraft must be navigated precisely at an enormous distance from Earth.

name: Enceladus Plume Sampling
what: Enceladus vents its subsurface ocean directly into space as plumes, so a spacecraft can sample ocean material without landing or drilling. It is the only known place where an ocean world delivers its chemistry to a passing probe.
how: A mission would either fly repeatedly through the plume at high velocity collecting ice grains, or land near a vent and collect fresh fallout, then analyse it with mass spectrometry and, in some architectures, return a sample to Earth. Plume encounter velocity and contamination control are the main design constraints.
companies: Johns Hopkins University Applied Physics Laboratory

name: Lightsail Interstellar Precursor
what: A laser-driven lightsail array would accelerate hundreds of gram-scale probes to a fraction of light speed for flyby reconnaissance of the nearest stars. It is the only architecture that reaches another system within a human lifetime using near-term physics.
how: A ground-based phased laser array pushes a metre-scale sail for several minutes, after which the probes coast, and a small fraction reach the target system and transmit data back with a compact laser or radio link. Atmosphere turbulence, sail survivability and the enormous receiver aperture needed for the return signal are the open problems.

name: Hydrothermal Chemosynthesis
what: Hydrothermal vent ecosystems run on chemical energy rather than sunlight, with microbes oxidising hydrogen sulphide, methane and hydrogen to fix carbon. They demonstrate that a biosphere does not require a star's light, only a chemical gradient.
how: Fluid circulating through hot rock reacts with minerals and emerges reduced, and chemolithoautotrophs harvest the disequilibrium between that fluid and seawater. The same redox chemistry is the leading candidate for life in Europa and Enceladus oceans.

name: Hycean World Atmospheric Survey
what: Warm sub-Neptunes with hydrogen-rich envelopes over liquid-water oceans are now prime targets for transmission spectroscopy. Telescope data have returned tentative detections of carbon-bearing molecules in several such worlds, though the signals remain contested and instrument-systematic limited.
how: As the planet transits its star, starlight filters through the atmosphere; the absorption depth at each wavelength encodes molecular composition, which Bayesian atmospheric models invert into mixing ratios and temperature structure.

name: Mars Sample Return Biosignature Chain
what: Cores cached by rovers would be returned to terrestrial laboratories for the most sensitive life-detection and dating instruments in existence, which cannot be miniaturised to flight mass. The programme has been restructured after cost growth.
how: A lander retrieves the cached tubes, an ascent vehicle launches them to Mars orbit, and a capture spacecraft carries them back to Earth for analysis under containment.

name: Interstellar Object Interception
what: Bodies such as 1I/Oumuamua and 2I/Borisov are unmodified remnants of other planetary systems, but they are discovered only weeks before passing perihelion. A pre-positioned interceptor could reach a newly found object and measure its composition directly.
how: A spacecraft parked in a low-energy orbit uses chemical or solar-electric propulsion to fly past the object, trading launch mass against arrival speed and available observation time.

name: Prebiotic Chemistry Reaction Networks
what: Experiments test whether nucleotides, amino acids and lipids can assemble from simple starting mixtures under plausible early-Earth or icy-moon conditions. The field has moved from isolated reactions to whole networks and the selection pressures that shape them.
how: Flow reactors hold mixtures at controlled temperature, pH and mineral surfaces while mass spectrometry tracks product populations and their evolution over time.

name: Exoplanet Phase-Curve Mapping
what: Thermal and reflected-light phase curves measure how an exoplanet's brightness varies through a full orbit, separating dayside emission from nightside emission and constraining heat redistribution, Bond albedo and wind-driven energy transport.
how: Space photometers and infrared spectrographs record continuous flux across the orbit; the amplitude, offset and shape of the curve reveal the day-night temperature contrast, the presence of clouds and the efficiency with which the atmosphere moves heat to the night side.

name: Titan Lake Organic Chemistry
what: Titan's polar lakes hold liquid methane and ethane carrying complex nitriles and hydrocarbons, forming a natural laboratory for prebiotic reaction networks in a solvent other than water.
how: A rotorcraft lands at multiple sites and samples lakebed and dune organics with a mass spectrometer and chemical analyser, testing whether amino-acid precursors and membrane-forming molecules assemble under cryogenic non-aqueous conditions.

name: Chirality Biosignature Detection
what: Terrestrial life uses almost exclusively left-handed amino acids and right-handed sugars, so a reproducible non-racemic excess of one handedness in an off-world sample is a strong biosignature that does not depend on assuming Earth-like biochemistry.
how: Chiral chromatography, circular dichroism and chiral-selective mass spectrometry separate enantiomers in a returned or in-situ sample; a departure from racemic abundance that cannot be explained by abiotic synthesis points toward a biological origin.

name: Nanopore Sequencing for Life Detection
use: In-situ polymer reading, sample return triage
what: Nanopore sequencers read informational polymers base by base as they thread a nanoscale pore, offering a compact, low-power route to sequence any genetic alphabet found off Earth rather than only the four bases used on Earth.
how: An applied voltage drives a strand through a protein or solid-state pore; each base produces a characteristic current blockade that is decoded in real time, and the same physical principle can in theory read non-terrestrial polymer chemistries.

name: Subglacial Lake Exploration
what: Beneath Antarctic ice sheets lie isolated liquid lakes sealed for millions of years, hosting microbial ecosystems that test the limits of habitability and serve as terrestrial analogues for Europa and Enceladus.
how: Clean hot-water drilling and sterilised probes breach the ice without introducing surface contaminants; the same forward-contamination and clean-access architecture is being adapted for cryobots targeting icy-moon oceans.

name: Transit Timing Variation Dynamics
what: Deviations of a planet's transit times from strict periodicity betray the gravitational pull of additional non-transiting planets, exposing systems that photometry alone would classify as single-planet.
how: Long-baseline photometric monitoring measures transit mid-points to within seconds; dynamical fits to the timing residuals recover the masses, periods and eccentricities of unseen companions and constrain the system's long-term stability.

name: Comet Cryogenic Sample Return
use: Primordial material analysis, origins of volatiles
what: Returning cryogenically preserved cometary material would deliver primordial ices and organics unaltered by atmospheric entry heating, giving the most direct available sample of the solar system's building blocks.
how: A concept mission rendezvouses with a comet, collects volatile-rich subsurface material into a cryogenic container and returns it with the sample held below sublimation temperature throughout cruise, entry and recovery.

name: Exoplanet Spectropolarimetry
what: Polarised light from an exoplanet carries information about cloud and haze particles that ordinary spectroscopy struggles to separate from the host star's signal and from instrumental systematics.
how: A high-contrast polarimeter measures the small polarised fraction of the combined star-planet light as the planet moves through its orbit; the polarisation phase curve constrains droplet size, particle shape and cloud altitude.

name: Ozone-Ultraviolet Biosignature Survey
what: Ozone produces a sharp ultraviolet absorption feature that is difficult to generate abiotically in large quantity, making the ultraviolet band an attractive place to search for an oxygen-rich atmosphere.
how: Ultraviolet spectrographs measure the depth of the ozone Hartley absorption band; combining its strength with methane abundance and the redox budget weighs whether an oxygen atmosphere is most plausibly biological.

name: Machine-Learning Biosignature Classification
what: Supervised models trained on synthetic spectra and known-Earth data can classify atmospheres as biotic or abiotic, flagging which candidates deserve scarce telescope time and quantifying the false-positive rate of each claim.
how: Generative models produce large libraries of plausible spectra for planets with and without life; a classifier learns the decision boundary between the classes and reports a calibrated probability rather than a binary verdict.

name: Deep Biosphere Analogue Drilling
what: Microbial life persists kilometres below the seafloor and continents, powered by radiolysis and geochemical gradients rather than sunlight, defining the outer limits of habitability without photosynthesis.
how: Ocean drilling and continental boreholes recover cores under anaerobic conditions; cell counts, isotope geochemistry and metagenomics establish standing biomass and identify the electron donors and acceptors sustaining it.

name: Exoplanet Transit Spectroscopy
what: Transmission spectroscopy now delivers molecular detections in exoplanet atmospheres at the micrometre level, including carbon dioxide, water, methane and sulphur dioxide. The method is the workhorse for deciding whether a world has a primary hydrogen envelope or a secondary, possibly rocky, atmosphere.
how: Starlight filtered through a planet atmosphere during transit carries absorption signatures; differencing in-transit against out-of-transit spectra isolates the planetary signal from the stellar one.

name: Radio Technosignature Survey
what: A sustained, multi-telescope survey scanning nearby stars and the Galactic plane for narrowband radio emission inconsistent with any natural astrophysical process.
how: Digital signal processing searches terahertz of bandwidth for drifting narrowband carriers, and candidates are re-observed by an independent telescope to reject terrestrial interference.

name: FAST Radio Technosignature Search
what: The largest single-dish radio telescope in the world contributes unmatched raw sensitivity to narrowband technosignature searches, particularly for faint repeating signals.
how: A five-hundred-metre active spherical reflector with a deformable cable net focuses on a feed cabin, and multibeam receivers digitise wide bands for coherent dedispersion and drift searches.

name: SKA Technosignature Search
what: A low-frequency aperture array with enormous field of view and survey speed will execute commensal technosignature searches across the entire accessible sky during ordinary astronomy operations.
how: Thousands of dipole antennas form digital beams on the sky; beamformed voltage data is fed to dedicated search backends running simultaneously with the primary science correlator.

name: Optical SETI
what: Cherenkov telescopes repurposed for astrophysics also hunt nanosecond optical pulses, the signature of an artificial laser beacon that would outshine the host star by orders of magnitude.
how: Large photon-collecting mirrors with nanosecond-resolution photodetectors look for coincident multi-telescope triggers that rule out cosmic-ray-induced flashes.

name: Machine-Learning Technosignature Detection
what: Convolutional and transformer models trained on injected synthetic signals now classify candidate narrowband events, cutting the human review load on petabytes of survey data.
how: Spectrogram patches are labelled with simulated drifting carriers and real interference, then a supervised network ranks live candidates, with classical algorithms as a control.

name: Coronagraphy and Starshade
what: Coronagraphy blocks a star's light inside the telescope to reveal faint companions, while a starshade flies tens of thousands of kilometres ahead as an external occulter. Together they enable direct imaging and spectroscopy of planets rather than indirect inference.
how: An internal coronagraph uses deformable mirrors and shaped pupils to suppress diffracted starlight, and a starshade blocks the star before light enters the aperture, removing diffraction at source. Both demand wavefront stability at the picometre level and precise formation flying in the starshade case.

name: Direct Imaging of Temperate Exoplanets
what: Coronagraphs and free-flying starshades suppress starlight by many orders of magnitude so a planet can be photographed directly rather than inferred from a transit. The payoff is access to non-transiting systems and to planets whose orbits never cross the stellar disc.
how: A starshade flown tens of thousands of kilometres ahead casts a shadow over the telescope aperture, while deformable mirrors in the coronagraph null the residual wavefront error down to the photon-noise floor.

name: Icy Moon Plume Sample Analysis
what: Plumes erupting from Enceladus and suspected at Europa carry ocean material into space where a flyby can sample it without landing. Analysis targets amino acids, lipids and chiral excesses that would be difficult to explain abiotically.
how: A mass spectrometer and capillary electrophoresis system ingest ice grains at kilometres per second, ionise them and separate molecules by mass and charge before detection.

name: Exomoon and Ring Detection
what: Moons and ring systems around exoplanets would appear as subtle timing and depth anomalies in transit light curves. Reported detections remain disputed because the required photometric precision sits at the edge of current capability.
how: Transit timing variations and out-of-transit dips are modelled against instrumental systematics, with repeated observations needed to confirm any periodic signal.

name: Comet Interceptor
what: A three-spacecraft ESA and JAXA mission that parks at the Sun-Earth L2 point and waits for a dynamically new comet entering the inner solar system. The main craft flies through the coma at up to 70 km per second while two small probes are released to sample different regions of the coma simultaneously.
how: The spacecraft loiters for up to three years so it can be retargeted to a comet that has never previously approached the Sun, preserving volatile chemistry unaltered by solar heating. Probes image the nucleus and dust environment during a brief high-velocity flyby.

name: Martian Moons eXploration
what: A JAXA-led sample return from the Martian moon Phobos using a super-resolution camera, laser altimeter and pneumatic corer to collect at least ten grams of regolith. The returned material would contain both Phobos material and ejected Martian surface rock.
how: The spacecraft performs quasi-satellite orbits around Phobos, releases a small rover to traverse the surface, and touches down briefly to core the regolith. The sample is sealed and returned inside a re-entry capsule.

name: Venus Aerobot Balloon
what: A superpressure helium balloon cruising in the Venus cloud deck at roughly 55 km altitude, where pressure and temperature approach Earth surface conditions. Payload concepts include a mass spectrometer, cloud particle instruments and a nephelometer to test for organic chemistry and the unknown ultraviolet absorber.
how: Superpressure design holds constant volume so altitude stays stable across the day-night cycle, and materials must resist sulfuric acid aerosols. Phase-change fluid concepts use day-night temperature swings to alter buoyancy and control altitude.

name: Titan Submarine
what: A submersible concept designed to traverse liquid methane and ethane seas on Titan and characterise dissolved organics, seafloor composition and wave dynamics. Its target is Kraken Mare, which exceeds 300 metres depth in places.
how: The vehicle must operate immersed in cryogenic hydrocarbon at 94 kelvin and 1.5 bar, and communicate to a surface lander by acoustic link because radio does not propagate through liquid methane. Power options include radioisotope thermal generators and batteries.

name: Triton Hopper
what: A hopping lander that harvests local nitrogen ice as propellant to relocate across Triton in kilometre-scale leaps, letting a single vehicle sample widely separated terrains instead of landing once.
how: Surface nitrogen ice is collected, heated and gasified, then expanded through a nozzle for propulsion. Low gravity and negligible atmosphere make ballistic hops energetically cheap relative to rover traverses.

name: Deep-Ultraviolet Raman Spectroscopy
what: Deep-ultraviolet Raman and fluorescence instruments on Mars rovers identify organic molecules and minerals at micrometre scale without sample preparation. The SHERLOC instrument on Perseverance maps organics and minerals in abraded rock surfaces with a 250 micrometre spot.
how: A 248 nanometre deep-UV laser excites Raman scattering; because fluorescence is largely avoided at deep-UV wavelengths, weak organic Raman bands remain detectable. Spectra are matched against a library of mineral and organic reference signatures.

name: Microfluidic Amino Acid Analyser
what: A lab-on-a-chip instrument designed to extract, fluorescently label and separate amino acids from a few cubic centimetres of liquid sample, detecting them at sub-nanomolar levels. It is intended to distinguish biological homochirality from abiotic racemic mixtures in ocean-world plume material.
how: Sample handling, labelling chemistry, capillary electrophoresis and laser-induced fluorescence detection are integrated on a single chip. Chiral separation resolves D and L enantiomers so the enantiomeric excess can be quantified.

name: X-ray Fluorescence Spectrometry
what: The PIXL instrument on Perseverance uses micro-focus X-ray fluorescence to map rock and soil elemental composition at about 100 micrometre resolution, quantifying major, minor and trace elements including chlorine, sulfur and strontium.
how: A focused X-ray beam excites atoms in the target and the emitted fluorescent X-rays carry energies characteristic of each element. Coupled contextual imaging registers elemental maps to visible rock texture.

name: Radiolytic Hydrogen Biosignatures
what: Investigation of whether hydrogen produced by water radiolysis in subsurface rock can sustain chemolithotrophic life on Mars and icy moons, and whether the resulting chemical fingerprints are detectable remotely. The process is documented in Precambrian shields and deep mine sites on Earth.
how: Natural radioactivity in crustal rock splits water into hydrogen and oxidants, providing a redox couple independent of sunlight. Detection targets include hydrogen and methane plumes, isotopic fractionation and diagnostic mineral alteration assemblages.

name: Tholin Haze Chemistry
what: Laboratory study of the complex organic aerosols produced when methane and nitrogen are irradiated in reducing atmospheres such as Titan's. The work tests whether haze particles hydrolyse into amino acids and nucleobases and whether they can mimic biological spectral signatures.
how: Gas mixtures are exposed to ultraviolet light or plasma discharge to grow analogue haze, then analysed by mass spectrometry and chromatography after hydrolysis. Resulting optical constants feed models of Titan and exoplanet haze.

name: Serpentinisation Hydrogen Production
what: Field and laboratory study of serpentinisation, the reaction of ultramafic rock with water that generates hydrogen and methane, as the geochemical engine behind alkaline hydrothermal ecosystems such as Lost City. It is a primary analogue for habitable chemistry on Enceladus and Europa.
how: Olivine and pyroxene react with seawater to form serpentine, magnetite and hydrogen, and the alkaline hydrogen-rich fluid drives abiotic organic synthesis and supports methanogens. Vent fluid and chimney sampling constrains the reaction network.

name: Galactic Habitable Zone Modelling
what: Models bounding the region of a galaxy where complex life is plausible by balancing the metallicity needed to build rocky planets against supernova and gamma-ray-burst sterilisation rates and the time available for evolution.
how: Stellar population synthesis and chemical evolution codes are combined with supernova rate maps and galactic dynamics to produce spatio-temporal habitability contours. Varying the assumptions identifies which galaxies could plausibly host observers.

name: Rare Earth Hypothesis Testing
what: Quantitative testing of the proposition that complex life requires a rare coincidence of planetary, orbital and galactic conditions such as a large stabilising moon, plate tectonics, a magnetic dynamo and a Jupiter-class impact shield.
how: Exoplanet demographic data, tidal and orbital evolution models and geodynamic simulations estimate how often each proposed prerequisite occurs and whether the conditions are genuinely independent requirements or correlated outcomes of the same process.

name: Lunar Farside Low-Frequency Radio Observatory
what: Radio astronomy conducted from the lunar farside, the only location shielded from terrestrial radio interference across the 1 to 50 megahertz band. That band carries the redshifted 21 centimetre signal from the cosmic dark ages and is a prime search space for narrowband artificial emission.
how: Antenna arrays are deployed on the farside or in a farside orbit so the Moon blocks Earth-directed interference. Instruments such as LuSEE-Night pathfind low-frequency receiver and antenna technology through the cryogenic lunar night.

name: Under-Ice Ocean Explorer AUV
what: Autonomous underwater vehicles designed to swim freely beneath an ice shell, reaching ocean volumes that a tethered cryobot cannot. Antarctic analogue vehicles have demonstrated long-range under-ice navigation, chemical sensing and sample capture, establishing the operational model for Europa and Enceladus.
how: The vehicle carries its own power and navigation, uses sonar and inertial dead reckoning away from acoustic beacons, and returns to a melt probe or docking station to recharge and transfer samples.

name: Planetary Cave and Lava Tube Astrobiology
what: Entering subsurface voids on Mars, the Moon and icy bodies, where shielding from radiation and oxidising dust preserves organic molecules that surface environments destroy. Lava tubes can span kilometres and hold stable temperatures and trapped ices for billions of years, making them the most probable accessible refuge for past or present life.
how: Rovers descend through skylight openings by tether or autonomous rappelling; lidar maps the void while contact instruments and drills sample wall coatings, floor dust and ice deposits.

name: Neutrino Astronomy and Planetary Tomography
what: Detecting neutrinos from stellar cores, supernovae and the Earth's interior, giving a direct view of processes that photons cannot escape. IceCube has already produced a neutrino image of the Galactic plane, and the technique extends to imaging the interior of a planet from the neutrinos it emits.
how: Kilometre-scale volumes of ice or water are instrumented with photomultipliers that catch faint Cherenkov light from neutrino interactions; direction and energy are reconstructed from photon arrival times.

name: Planetary Radar Astronomy
what: Bouncing high-power radio waves off asteroids, planets and moons to measure shape, spin, surface roughness and near-surface density at metre resolution. Radar is the only ground-based technique that can image the internal structure of a near-Earth asteroid, and it is decisive for any deflection campaign.
how: A large transmitter sends a coded continuous signal; the echo is received by the same dish or a distant one, and delay-Doppler processing converts it into a resolved image.

name: Atmospheric Escape and Mass Loss
what: Measuring the rate at which hydrogen, helium and heavier species escape from exoplanet atmospheres, which decides whether a planet keeps its volatiles and remains habitable. Helium at 1083 nanometres is the most accessible tracer and has now been detected around dozens of transiting planets.
how: Spectrographs record absorption in the lines escaping gas produces during transit, and stellar activity is modelled and subtracted so that the planetary mass-loss signal can be isolated.

name: Exoplanet Volcanism Detection
what: Identifying active volcanism on rocky exoplanets through sulphur dioxide, sulphur monoxide and other short-lived species that must be continuously replenished to remain detectable. Tentative volcanic signatures have already been reported for a tidally heated Earth-sized world, opening a new branch of comparative planetology.
how: Transmission and emission spectroscopy search for sulphur-bearing gases and thermal emission excess, which are then compared against tidal dissipation and outgassing models to test whether the source is genuinely volcanic.

name: Minimal Synthetic Cell
what: Cells built from the smallest genome that can sustain growth and division, assembled from defined chemical components, used to establish the minimum functional requirements of life. Minimal cells are also clean chassis for testing which genetic circuits are essential rather than merely useful.
how: A chemically synthesised genome is transplanted into an emptied cell envelope; iterative deletion with growth monitoring compresses the genome to its functional minimum.

name: Mirror-Image Life Biosafety
what: Assessing the risk of organisms built from mirror-image biomolecules, which would evade most natural predators and immune recognition and could therefore spread without check. Technical reviews have concluded that mirror bacteria are not yet constructible but that the remaining barriers are falling steadily.
how: Researchers track the falling cost of building mirror proteins, mirror ribosomes and mirror genomes, and model how a mirrored organism would interact with natural ecosystems and immune systems.

name: Xeno Nucleic Acids
what: Nucleic acid analogues with alternative backbones or sugars that store and evolve genetic information but are not substrates for natural enzymes. Engineered polymerases can translate between XNA and DNA, which lets researchers select and evolve molecules that natural biology cannot copy and test whether heredity is unique to terrestrial chemistry.
how: Engineered polymerases synthesise XNA strands, and in vitro selection then evolves XNA aptamers and catalysts whose behaviour reports on the chemistry's capacity to support information storage.
companies: Medical Research Council Laboratory of Molecular Biology

name: Interstellar Panspermia Modelling
what: Quantifying whether life could travel between star systems on dust, comets or artificial carriers, and what that would imply for how biology is distributed across the galaxy. Ejection rates, radiation survival, transit time and capture probability combine into a single transfer likelihood that can be tested against the observed distribution of habitable worlds.
how: Dynamical simulations of ejection and capture are coupled to radiation-damage experiments on terrestrial and Martian analogue organisms, producing maps of where transfer is plausible and where it is not.

name: Rogue Planet Habitability
what: Free-floating planets appear to outnumber stars in the galaxy, and a subset could sustain liquid oceans under ice from internal heat alone. A planet that needs no star would redefine the habitable zone and enlarge the plausible volume of inhabited real estate by orders of magnitude.
how: Microlensing surveys estimate rogue planet abundance and mass distribution, while thermal and tidal models calculate whether radiogenic and tidal heating can keep subsurface water liquid over billions of years.

name: Artificial Wormhole Generation for Interstellar Travel
what: Creates traversable Einstein‑Rosen bridges using high‑energy plasma conduits stabilized by exotic matter fields.
how: A lattice of superconducting rings generates negative energy densities via Casimir‑engineered vacuum states, forming a temporary throat that links two distant points.

name: Galaxy‑Scale Biosphere Engineering
use: Seed life across the Milky Way
what: Launches autonomous terraforming probes equipped with engineered extremophiles to colonise rogue planets and interstellar clouds.
how: Probes synthesize atmospheric gases, deposit nutrient matrices, and continuously monitor biosignature evolution via embedded quantum sensors.

name: Kuiper Belt Object Flyby
what: Close flyby reconnaissance of Kuiper Belt objects beyond 30 AU, resolving surface geology, colour diversity and binary structure in a population that has stayed near-pristine since accretion. New Horizons proved the class with its Arrokoth encounter, returning the most primitive planetary surface yet imaged.
how: A spacecraft coasts on a heliocentric trajectory for years, then captures a short high-phase-angle and low-phase-angle imaging sequence inside a flyby window of hours, with optical navigation retargeting to the chosen body and a downlink stretched over months.

name: Solar Oberth Maneuver Probe
what: A perihelion pass extremely close to the Sun converts orbital energy into a very high heliocentric speed, enabling outer-planet and Kuiper Belt arrival times several times shorter than conventional gravity assists allow. The engineering cost is a thermal protection system that survives intense solar flux while the spacecraft is still operating.
how: The probe falls inward on a low-perihelion orbit, executes its main burn at perihelion where the Oberth effect maximises energy gained per unit of propellant, then coasts outbound with the science payload protected behind a shield during the encounter phase.

name: Laser Frequency Comb Exoplanet Spectrograph
what: Provides an absolute wavelength reference at precision high enough to measure stellar reflex motion of a few centimetres per second, the level needed to detect Earth-mass planets in habitable zones. It also removes instrumental drift as a systematic floor in long radial-velocity campaigns.
how: A mode-locked laser emits thousands of evenly spaced optical lines anchored to a stabilised reference, and those lines are filtered into the spectrograph alongside starlight so each pixel is calibrated against a known wavelength rather than a laboratory lamp.

name: Exoplanet Magnetic Field Detection
what: Measures the magnetism of planets around other stars, which governs whether an atmosphere survives stellar wind erosion over geological time. Auroral radio bursts, transit Lyman-alpha absorption and bow-shock geometry are the three observable handles.
how: Low-frequency radio arrays monitor planet-hosting systems for coherent polarised emission modulated at the planet orbital or rotation period, while ultraviolet spectrographs measure anomalous Lyman-alpha transit depth that indicates an extended magnetospheric interaction.

name: Exocomet and Debris Disk Transit Monitoring
use: Volatile delivery and planetary system dynamics
what: Tracks aperiodic absorption events produced by evaporating exocomets crossing the face of their host star, revealing the volatile inventory of a planetary system and the rate at which water is delivered inward. The events are short and unpredictable, so the science depends on dedicated high-cadence monitoring rather than survey data.
how: High-resolution spectroscopy detects variable redshifted calcium absorption lasting hours, and simultaneous time-series photometry measures the accompanying dimming and constrains the gas-to-dust ratio of the disintegrating body.

name: Isotopic Biosignature Analysis
use: Life detection, ancient Earth and Mars sample analysis
what: Measures stable isotope ratios such as carbon-13 depletion and sulfur-34 fractionation in ancient sediments and Martian rocks, because metabolic pathways generate fractionations that abiotic chemistry rarely reproduces at the same magnitude. Isotopic evidence survives metamorphism that destroys molecular biosignatures.
how: Evolved gas analysis in a sealed oven liberates volatiles for mass spectrometric separation of isotopologues, while secondary-ion mass spectrometry and laser ablation map ratios at micrometre scale within individual mineral grains.

name: Lipid Biomarker Analysis
use: Life detection, microbial ecology, deep-time biosignatures
what: Extracts and identifies membrane lipids and their diagenetic products from ancient rocks, since lipid carbon skeletons are diagnostic of specific microbial groups and persist far longer than nucleic acids. Hopanes and steranes record the presence of bacteria and eukaryotes in rocks billions of years old.
how: Solvent extraction and derivatisation feed gas chromatography coupled to mass spectrometry, which resolves individual molecular fossils, and compound-specific isotope analysis then ties each molecule to the carbon fixation pathway that produced it.

name: Artificial Illumination Technosignature
what: Searches for nightside city-scale illumination on exoplanets, a signature that requires no deliberate transmission and therefore widens the technosignature search beyond beacons aimed at us. Its value is that it correlates with population and energy use rather than with intent to communicate.
how: High-contrast imaging and phase-curve photometry measure a nightside flux excess in spectral bands where natural thermal emission is minimal, and the measured spectral shape is compared against model illumination spectra and against natural alternatives such as volcanism.

name: Waste Heat Technosignature
what: A civilisation must radiate the entropy of every joule it uses, so a planet, moon or engineered structure should show mid-infrared excess above the equilibrium temperature set by its star. The signature is thermodynamic rather than behavioural, which makes it hard to avoid for any large-scale energy economy.
how: Mid-infrared photometry and spectroscopy measure thermal emission across the phase curve, and the result is tested against radiative-transfer models of natural surfaces, atmospheres and dust to separate engineering from geology.

name: Atmospheric Pollution Technosignature
what: Targets industrial gases such as chlorofluorocarbons and nitrogen dioxide that have no significant natural source, making them far less ambiguous than oxygen or methane, both of which have abiotic production routes. Detection would be evidence of technology rather than of biology.
how: Transmission and emission spectroscopy of transiting and directly imaged planets searches for narrow absorption features at the wavelengths those molecules occupy, and atmospheric retrieval models extract abundances while testing stellar contamination and instrument systematics as alternative explanations.

name: Gravitational-Wave Technosignature Search
what: Examines gravitational-wave catalogues for signals that cannot plausibly come from astrophysical mergers, such as long-lived monochromatic emission or anomalous chirp structure from engineered compact objects. It is the one technosignature channel that does not rely on electromagnetic radiation at all.
how: Matched-filter and continuous-wave searches run over interferometer data for parameters outside the known compact-binary population, and candidate events are cross-checked against astrophysical formation models before being flagged.

name: Protoplanetary Disk Chemistry with ALMA
use: Tracing the raw material of habitable planets
what: Millimetre and submillimetre interferometry that maps the chemical inventory of planet-forming disks, detecting water, methanol, complex organics and nitriles in the exact reservoirs that later become comets and planets. It links interstellar chemistry in cold clouds to the volatile content of the worlds that form.
how: Dozens of antennas are correlated into a single aperture and molecular rotational lines at millimetre wavelengths are separated by rest frequency. The spatial distribution of each species is recovered from the visibilities, revealing rings, snowlines and asymmetries around young stars.

name: Exoplanet Host-Star Contamination in Transmission Spectra
use: Ruling out false positives in atmosphere claims
what: The diagnostic work that separates absorption by a planet atmosphere from absorption by unocculted starspots, faculae and stellar activity crossing the transit chord. Ignoring it can manufacture a water or methane detection that is really a stellar artefact, so it is a mandatory step before any habitability claim.
how: Simultaneous photometry during transit flags spot-crossing events, high-resolution spectroscopy resolves line shapes to distinguish stellar from planetary lines, and spot models are fitted jointly with retrieved atmospheric parameters to bound contamination.

name: Active SETI and Interstellar Message Design
what: The design, governance and ethics of deliberately transmitting detectable signals toward nearby stars rather than only listening. It forces explicit choices about message content, target selection, beacon encoding and who is entitled to speak for humanity, and it is the most contested area of the search for life.
how: Proposals combine mathematical primers, physical constants, prime-number and pixel-grid encodings on radio or optical carriers aimed at nearby Sun-like systems and habitable-zone candidates, with debate centred on risk, reversibility and international consultation.

name: Lunar Polar Organic Preservation
use: Searching for prebiotic chemistry in cold traps
what: The study of permanently shadowed lunar polar craters as cold, radiation-shielded archives that may have preserved volatile organics delivered by comets and asteroids for billions of years. With no atmosphere or liquid water to destroy them, lunar polar samples test whether the raw ingredients of life survive long-term in the inner solar system.
how: Permanently shadowed regions hold ices at tens of kelvin, so a rover or sample-return mission drills volatile-bearing regolith, seals samples in cold curation, and analyses them for amino acids, chirality and isotopic signatures using mass spectrometry and liquid chromatography in a thermally controlled chain.

name: Planetary Protection and Sample Containment
use: Sample return, forward and backward contamination limits
what: The engineering and policy framework that keeps Earth life from contaminating other worlds and keeps returned samples from contaminating Earth. It determines which landing sites are permissible, how spacecraft are sterilised, and how a Mars or comet sample is sealed, transported and opened under containment.
how: Forward protection uses cleanroom assembly, bioburden reduction and trajectory analysis to bound the probability of landing viable organisms. Backward protection uses hermetic seals, witness plates, negative-pressure gloveboxes and high-containment laboratories with life-detection assays before any sample is distributed.

name: Search for Extraterrestrial Artefacts
use: Detecting physical relics of non-human technology in the Solar System
what: A systematic survey of the lunar surface, Earth co-orbitals, Lagrange points and near-Earth space for objects that cannot be explained by natural geology or human activity. Unlike radio SETI, which listens for signals, artefact search looks for durable hardware, which could survive for geological timescales and therefore cannot be ruled out by the fact that no signal is currently being transmitted
how: High-resolution orbital imaging is compared against models of impact and volcanic geology, radar and thermal mapping is used to flag anomalous subsurface structure, and candidate objects are triaged spectroscopically. Debris from interstellar meteors recovered from the ocean floor provides a complementary physical sample.
